The binding defect makes resolution of that disputed determination unnecessary; the Court does not find that no relevant issue was ever decided.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Uncertainty about every notice, authorization or control fact requires no exploratory remand or adverse factual finding. A genuinely available defense or constitutionally valid binding relationship remains subject to its own proof, preservation and procedural requirements. No new theory or finding that one exists is guaranteed. No state-count ruling, earlier Tax Injunction Act dismissal, properly binding judgment or separate Buck Act claim is reopened.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Reversed and remanded, 9–0, as to the dispositive nonparty bar on Richards and Hill's reviewed federal claims. Ordinary legally available defenses, valid preclusion and remedy conditions remain; there is no mandatory discovery, representative-adequacy hearing or opportunity to construct a new preclusion theory. No immediate trial, tax invalidation, refund, damages, injunction or eventual recovery is ordered or guaranteed.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** No Supreme Court precedent is overruled; the constitutional prerequisite to binding these nonparties defeats both proposed forms of preclusion without extending collateral review or reopening otherwise binding judgments.

### Prison access and prospective relief

#### Lewis v. Casey, 518 U.S. 343 (1996)

**Docket or dockets:** No. 94-1511.
**Decided:** June 24, 1996.

##### Whether books alone satisfy the right of meaningful access

**Holding:** Bounds requires a meaningful practical opportunity for court access through effective libraries, trained assistance or other effective arrangements considered as a whole; adequate books do not discharge that duty for prisoners unable to use them without needed assistance. It guarantees neither a preferred library program, physical browsing in every case, professional counsel for every prisoner nor the decree's numerical requirements.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy’s Part I, unanimous.

**Material application:** Bartholic’s dismissal and Harris’s inability to file establish actual obstruction at their supported scope. An inventory-based paging system with prompt delivery may work for prisoners capable of independent use; that conditional possibility proves neither Arizona’s actual adequacy nor adequacy for differing literacy or language needs.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No fixed number of all injured prisoners, right to ultimate success, constitutional library specification or automatic appointed counsel is established.

##### What connection to a legal claim is required for access liability

**Holding:** A Bounds access-liability claim requires actual or evidence-supported imminent hindrance of a qualifying, nonfrivolous legal claim, subject to the validity of restrictions reasonably related to legitimate penological interests. The prisoner need not win the obstructed case or complete an impossible filing, but a deficient inventory, preferred staffing arrangement or abstract wish for better research does not alone establish the violation.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy’s Part II, joined by Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Scalia and Thomas; five Justices.

**Material application:** Technical dismissal, inability to file a contemplated qualifying claim or sufficiently concrete threatened obstruction can supply the connection. A procedural defect does not itself make the underlying claim substantively frivolous. Evidence and reasonable inferences may prove the real claim and obstacle before avoidable filing failure.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The additional Article III preliminary-merits screen, subgroup-standing requirement and categorical sentence/conditions and initial-filing restrictions have only four votes. Ordinary Lujan injury, causation and stage-appropriate proof remain. Genuine state-created-liberty claims remain possible under Sandin; no categorical exclusion of every other retained right, universal end of assistance upon filing or general private-litigation subsidy is adopted. Independent communications and petition claims retain their own predicates.

##### What proof and governmental role support classwide prison-access relief

**Holding:** Common relief must correspond to a demonstrated common barrier and an identified affected group; individual obstruction or a resource deficiency alone does not establish an unrestricted statewide violation. Relief must respect restrictions reasonably related to legitimate penological interests and give the State a genuine opportunity to devise an effective cure, while permitting measures actually necessary to repair the proved wrong.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy’s Part III, joined by Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer; eight Justices.

**Material application:** Common evidence may prove a common barrier without proof that every class member has already lost a suit, but geographical and functional reach require support. The actual findings do not establish a denial at every facility or independent broad entitlements for all non-English-speaking or lockdown prisoners. Opportunity to rebut a presumptive Gluth statewide template did not supply Arizona’s genuine initial remedial design role.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Turner requires examination of the actual reasonable relationship to legitimate penological interests with appropriate deference; injury alone does not invalidate a valid restriction, and merely asserting security does not establish validity. Jenkins permits necessary repair measures without making every remedial detail a freestanding constitutional right.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Unsupported classwide approval set aside and remanded, 8–1; Stevens accepts a narrower remedial remand. Established obstruction, supported findings and common evidence remain. No unrestricted statewide violation, automatic dismissal or fixed library, telephone, staffing or resource minimum.

##### How original PLRA §802 governs this existing prospective decree and any replacement

**Holding:** Section 802 applies amended section 3626 to prospective relief granted before, on or after April 26, 1996; relief here requires findings that it is narrowly drawn, extends no further than necessary to correct the federal-right violation of the particular plaintiffs, and is the least intrusive means necessary, with substantial weight given to adverse effects on public safety or criminal-justice-system operation. Relief exceeding official state-law authority or otherwise violating state or local law additionally requires federal permission, necessity to correct the federal violation, and absence of any other corrective relief.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy’s Part IV, joined by all eight Associate Justices; Stone-Zsela agrees only with the statutory remand disposition.

**Material application:** Amended §3626 applies to relief granted before, on or after April 26, 1996. Prospective relief means relief other than compensatory monetary damages. This prison-conditions action is not excluded habeas merely because access assistance facilitates habeas. Existing findings may satisfy actual predicates without ritual wording; reasonable cost or absence of hardship does not substitute for need, narrowness and least intrusiveness.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Section 3626(a)(1)(B)’s federal-permission, necessity and no-other-relief conditions govern state/local-law conflicts separately from (A). Subsection (C) supplies no authority to build prisons or raise taxes and preserves existing limits. New preliminary relief must be otherwise authorized and satisfy narrowness, need, least intrusiveness, safety and the separate state-law terms; it expires ninety days after entry unless the required prospective findings are made and the order made final before expiration. The former permanent decree is not automatically a new preliminary order. No constitutional challenge to §802 or prisoner-release remedy is decided.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Prospective-decree approval set aside and remanded, 9–0 in disposition, eight on statutory reasoning. Actual findings, alternatives, improvements and security must be considered; the decree is neither automatically retained nor dissolved.

**Later-authority backlinks:** Plyler v. Moore, Fourth Circuit No. 96-6884, 1997-06-23, resolves the reserved Article III challenge to §3626(b)(2) only with the original (b)(3) current-or-ongoing safeguard; see Constitutional Structure — Congressional amendment of law governing prospective relief. Pub. L. 105-119, §123(a)(1)(A), (b), effective 1997-11-26, changes the federal-law condition for state/local-law-conflicting prospective relief and applies it to pending cases.

**Current-force modification:** Effective November 26, 1997, including pending cases, Pub. L. 105-119, §123(a)(1)(A), 111 Stat. 2470, changes §3626(a)(1)(B)(i) from federal permission to federal requirement: the relief that exceeds state/local authority or violates state/local law must be required by federal law, with the separate necessity and no-other-corrective-relief conditions retained. The announced Holding states the original text and remains its construction; the amendment supplies the later statutory condition without altering the prior adjudication.

##### When termination and an automatic stay arise under the original §3626

**Holding:** The original section 3626 termination provisions do not dissolve relief merely upon enactment: the immediate-termination entitlement for relief entered without the required findings remains subject to written, record-based findings that relief is necessary to correct a current OR ongoing federal-right violation and remains narrowly drawn, no broader than necessary, and least intrusive. The automatic stay requires an actual pending qualifying motion and runs only for the original statutory period described below.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy’s Part IV, joined by all eight Associate Justices; Stone-Zsela agrees only with the statutory remand disposition.

**Material application:** Under (b)(1), a party or intervener may seek termination after the applicable two years from relief, one year after denial under that paragraph, or two years after enactment for preenactment relief; earlier agreement is permitted. Under (b)(2), a defendant or intervener is entitled to immediate termination absent the original required findings, subject to (b)(3)’s written record findings of necessary, narrowly drawn, no-broader-than-necessary and least-intrusive relief for a current OR ongoing violation. Subsection (b)(4) preserves earlier relief available under other law.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Modification/termination motions must be decided promptly. Original (e) stays the challenged relief from day thirty after a pending (b)(1)/(b)(2) motion, or day 180 for a motion under other law, until the final order resolving it. No such filing is established. Consent decrees remain subject to (a); private agreements enforceable federally only by reinstating the settled proceeding are distinct, with available state breach remedies preserved. Relief entered by state courts solely on state claims is outside the statute.

**Operative remedy or transition:** No termination or automatic stay is entered by enactment or this remand.

**Current-force modification:** Effective November 26, 1997, including pending cases, Pub. L. 105-119, §123(a)(2)–(3), (b), 111 Stat. 2470–2471, replaces §3626(b)(3)’s current-or-ongoing condition with current and ongoing, retaining the written record findings and need, narrowness and least-intrusiveness requirements. The amended §3626(e)(1) provides that mandamus shall lie to remedy any failure to issue a prompt ruling; (e)(2) makes a motion to modify or terminate prospective relief under (b) operate as the prescribed stay, retaining the statutory thirty-day and 180-day timing branches and final-order endpoint. New (e)(3) permits postponing the stay’s effective date by no more than sixty days for good cause, excluding general calendar congestion. Under new (e)(4), orders staying, suspending, delaying or barring that stay, apart from the (e)(3) postponement, are appealable under §1292(a)(1) as orders refusing to dissolve or modify an injunction regardless of their name or preliminary/final designation. The original-text holding remains unchanged for its earlier operation; the enactment supplies no individual motion, stay or deadline and resolves no constitutional challenge.

**Later-authority backlinks:** Pub. L. 105-119, §123(a)(2)–(3), (b), effective 1997-11-26, pending-case termination-preservation and stay amendments. Inmates of Suffolk County Jail v. Rouse, First Circuit Nos. 97-1261, 97-1262, 97-1263 and 97-1334, decided 1998-01-15, applies the amended preservation condition where no violation qualifying only under the broader original condition is identified.

##### What conditions govern continued special-master assistance

**Holding:** A special master in this prison-conditions remedy must be disinterested and objective, give due regard to public safety, and be warranted by a finding of sufficient remedial complexity; appointments, compensation, work and continued need must comply with section 3626(f)'s separate conditions below. Those requirements apply to the master's statutory role regardless of title and do not themselves establish misconduct or invalidate every prior act or accrued fee.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy’s Part IV, joined by all eight Associate Justices; Stone-Zsela agrees only with the statutory remand disposition.

**Material application:** A necessary appointment under (f) requires each side to submit up to five names, each may strike up to three opposing names, and the court chooses among those remaining; the prescribed partiality interlocutory appeal remains. Compensation is capped at the §3006A appointed-counsel hourly rate plus reasonable costs, paid from Judiciary appropriations. Continuing need must be reviewed every six months. Hearings and proposed findings are on the record; ex parte findings and communications are forbidden. A master may assist remedial plans and be removed at any time, and service ends upon termination of relief. Title alone cannot evade the statutory role.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The prior opportunity to challenge fees survives. Accrued-fee and temporal questions remain for adjudication; no misconduct, retrospective invalidity of every prior act, repayment or automatic new appointment is established.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- **Bounds v. Smith, 430 U.S. 817, and Wolff v. McDonnell, 418 U.S. 539:** Preserve meaningful access and effective methods rather than a constitutional library specification. Bounds is not overruled; four proposed categorical limits do not become Court law.
- **Murray v. Giarratano, 492 U.S. 1:** Preserves choice among effective assistance arrangements without a general right to appointed counsel for every prisoner.
- **Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, June 12, 1992, and City of Los Angeles v. Lyons, 461 U.S. 95:** Preserve personal injury, causation, appropriate prospective exposure and proof at the litigation stage. The Court does not adopt the four-Justice preliminary merits screen or decide standing in gross from a party concession.
- **Turner v. Safley, 482 U.S. 78:** Applies reasonable relationship to legitimate penological interests, with actual examination and proper deference rather than automatic acceptance of a security assertion.
- **Missouri v. Jenkins, June 12, 1995:** Applies violation-linked repair while preserving implementation measures necessary to correct a proved wrong. Each means need not independently violate the Constitution.
- **Rufo v. Inmates of Suffolk County Jail, 502 U.S. 367:** Preserves lawful responsive modification; the new statute's distinct mandatory requirements must also be applied.
- **Sandin v. Conner, June 19, 1995:** Preserves its actual rule for meaningful state-created prison liberty under genuine substantive constraints. No categorical hardship replacement is imported to exclude access to those claims.
- **Madsen v. Women's Health Center, Inc., June 30, 1994:** Preserves connection between remedial terms and their predicate; its speech-specific standard is not a universal least-restrictive-means rule or a substitute for section 3626.

No precedent is overruled. Gluth's earlier remedy supplies background and a proposed template, not a finding of statewide injury in this record.

#### Plyler v. Moore

**Docket or dockets:** Fourth Circuit No. 96-6884; no separate Supreme Court docket assigned.

**Decided:** 1997-06-23.

For the Article III validity of the conditional termination rule, see Plyler v. Moore, Fourth Circuit No. 96-6884, decided 1997-06-23, Constitutional Structure — Congressional amendment of law governing prospective relief.

##### I. The original PLRA supplies an independent, conditional termination rule

**Holding:** For covered federal prison-conditions prospective relief, including relief entered before April 26, 1996, original §3626(b)(2) entitles a defendant or intervener to immediate termination when the relief was approved without findings that it was narrowly drawn, extended no further than necessary to correct the federal-right violation and was the least intrusive necessary means. Under original §3626(b)(3), relief must nevertheless continue upon written, record-based findings that it remains necessary to correct a current **or** ongoing federal violation, is no broader than necessary, and is narrowly drawn and the least intrusive means; existing substantive findings may satisfy the statute without ritual wording.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's opinion of the Court is joined in full by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. All nine directly adopt the following rules and qualifications.

**Material application:** Section 802 expressly reaches existing prospective relief. The State must establish the termination basis and the court must independently apply (b)(3); missing ritual phrases, age of the decree or relief exceeding constitutional minima alone does not establish dispensability.

**Limits and questions not reached:** This is (b)(2) termination, not the waiting-period route under (b)(1) or automatic stay under (e). The legal appeal establishes neither a preserved failure to consider qualifying findings nor a supported violation requiring a new hearing; no statewide compliance finding or accrued monetary liability is decided.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Lewis supplies the complete original findings and preservation conditions. Rufo remains the equitable modification rule, but its significant-change threshold is no additional prerequisite to this independent statutory route.

**Current-force modification:** From November 26, 1997, including pending cases, Pub. L. 105-119, §123(a)(2), (b), 111 Stat. 2470–2471, requires a current and ongoing federal-right violation under §3626(b)(3), instead of the original current-or-ongoing condition. The independent (b)(2) route and the substantive written-findings, need, narrowness and least-intrusiveness requirements remain. The announced Holding continues to state the original-text rule; the amendment does not rewrite that adjudication.

**Later-authority backlinks:** Pub. L. 105-119, §123(a)(2), (b), effective 1997-11-26, changes the preservation condition for pending cases. Inmates of Suffolk County Jail v. Rouse, First Circuit Nos. 97-1261, 97-1262, 97-1263 and 97-1334, decided 1998-01-15, applies the amended condition without deciding a case where the changed conjunction excludes an otherwise supported violation.

##### III. Negotiated decree protections are not automatically independent federal rights

**Holding:** Incorporating agreed protections into a federal consent decree does not make every protection exceeding underlying federal law the independent federal right whose violation prevents termination under §3626(b)(2). Continuing prospective enforcement remains subject to the statute, while relief necessary to correct an actual federal violation must be preserved under the full original (b)(3) conditions.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's opinion of the Court is joined in full by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. All nine directly adopt the following rules and qualifications.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Relief exceeding a constitutional minimum may still be necessary to correct an actual federal violation. Separate contractual or state-law claims and independently accrued rights are not adjudicated.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Rufo permits negotiated obligations beyond constitutional minima without insulating their future enforcement from valid legislation. Lewis permits necessary corrective measures; Joseph A.'s performance-condition ruling, made without a PLRA prison-conditions predicate, does not displace this statutory route.

**Current-force modification:** The distinction between negotiated decree terms and independent federal rights remains controlling. For the preservation condition incorporated in this proposition, Pub. L. 105-119, §123(a)(2), (b), effective November 26, 1997 and applicable to pending cases, substitutes current and ongoing for current or ongoing; the other preservation requirements remain. The full statutory transition appears in this case’s independent-termination question above.

**Later-authority backlinks:** Pub. L. 105-119, §123(a)(2), (b), effective 1997-11-26, changes the incorporated preservation condition; Inmates of Suffolk County Jail v. Rouse, decided 1998-01-15, applies the amended condition and preserves the decree/right distinction.

##### IV. The presented due-process claim does not bar termination

**Holding:** Beneficiaries of this mutable prospective decree have no vested entitlement to perpetual federal enforcement of its unchanged terms despite valid later law. On the presented legal challenge, the judicial motion process, opportunity to oppose termination and appellate review satisfy due process; no additional evidentiary remand follows from an unestablished possibility that a statutory preservation condition was overlooked.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's opinion of the Court is joined in full by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. All nine directly adopt the following rules and qualifications.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No unrecorded hearing is presumed or actual denial of an opportunity to present a preserved factual claim adjudicated. A demonstrated failure to apply (b)(3) would be distinct, and state sovereignty would not excuse it. General equal protection, accrued or contractual rights, other PLRA provisions and particular current prison conditions remain undecided.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Termination of prospective federal enforcement is affirmed unanimously against the presented legal objections. No new hearing, automatic stay, prisoner-release order, accrued-damages cancellation or extinguishment of independent rights follows.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Lewis's meaningful-access and original current-or-ongoing protections remain operative.

#### Inmates of Suffolk County Jail v. Rouse

**Docket or dockets:** First Circuit Nos. 97-1261, 97-1262, 97-1263 and 97-1334; no separate Supreme Court docket stated.

**Decided:** 1998-01-15.

For the Article III validity of the prospective-law change, see Inmates of Suffolk County Jail v. Rouse, First Circuit Nos. 97-1261, 97-1262, 97-1263 and 97-1334, decided January 15, 1998, Constitutional Structure — Congressional amendment of law governing prospective relief.

##### The independent statutory termination route and amended preservation condition govern

**Holding:** Section 3626(b)(2) permits termination of covered prospective prison-conditions relief approved without the substantive need, narrowness and least-intrusiveness findings. The State must establish that predicate. Existing actual findings can suffice without ritual statutory wording, and Rufo's separate equitable significant-change threshold is not an additional prerequisite. Under §3626(b)(3), as amended effective November 26, 1997 and applicable to pending cases, preservation requires written, record-based findings of necessity to correct a current and ongoing federal-right violation, with relief no broader than necessary, narrowly drawn and least intrusive. Consent decrees and pretrial-detention conditions are covered. Negotiated terms are not automatically independent federal rights, but necessary corrective relief may exceed the minimum conduct rule.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's Part I, unanimous.

##### The supported findings assessment permits termination without a speculative new inquiry

**Holding:** The reported judicial evaluation establishes no qualifying findings or supported federal violation requiring preservation of this relief. No violation meeting the broader original condition but excluded by the amended conjunction is identified. The narrower text therefore creates no outcome-determinative difference on this record.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's Part I, unanimous.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Independent judicial review and a proper opportunity to offer relevant evidence remain required. Evaluated reports and existing findings support termination here; no qualifying violation under the broader original condition is identified. No permanent compliance finding or new hearing follows from speculative deterioration.


##### Vested-right and procedural due process do not preserve unchanged future enforcement

**Holding:** Beneficiaries possess no perpetual entitlement to federal enforcement of the mutable decree's unchanged prospective terms against valid later remedial law. The reported motion, opposition and review support rejection of the presented procedural objection.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's Part III, unanimous.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Past lawful effects and independently accrued claims are preserved. Calling continuing judicial obligations contractual does not exempt them from the governing termination conditions.

##### The assumed independent contract-impairment objection fails at its presented scope

**Holding:** Assuming a contract and substantial impairment solely to decide the objection, the federal-nonparty rationality framework permits this restriction on continuing federal supervision. The United States does not become a contracting party merely because a federal court approved the decree or Congress enacted legislation benefiting States.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's Part IV has all eight Associates; Stone-Zsela agrees only in rejecting the objection.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Neither a separate contract’s existence, survival, breach or enforceability nor accrued contractual liability is decided.

##### The presented equality challenge fails without diminishing pretrial rights or meaningful access

**Holding:** Ordinary rational review permits the statute's restriction on continuing prison-decree supervision because it reasonably relates the actual supervisory disadvantage to legitimate institutional responsibility and resource concerns while retaining enforceable federal-right protection.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's Part III, unanimous.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Pretrial protection under Bell and meaningful court access remain; nonsuspect status alone does not prove validity, and no blanket prohibition on supported threatened-injury relief is adopted.

##### Termination ends prospective judicial operation, not past adjudication

**Holding:** The statutory direction to terminate, together with the inclusion of consent decrees in prospective relief, requires ending the decree's continuing judicial obligations themselves. It does not declare the original judgment erroneous, erase completed determinations or payments, or retrospectively vacate lawful past effects.

**Proposition-level authority:** All nine join the prospective/historical distinction; Kennedy's Part V ordinary-affirmance mandate has all eight Associates.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The separate Rule 60(b) theory was set aside conditionally upon obtaining termination; its merits remain unaddressed once that condition is satisfied.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The First Circuit judgment is affirmed, including termination of the decree’s future operation without retrospective annulment. No new merits inquiry, hearing, release, automatic stay or deadline is ordered.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

Plyler supplies the independent statutory route, judicial preservation inquiry and bounded constitutional operation under its original text; the present amendment is applied without rewriting that holding. Lewis retains the statute's scope, transition, findings and meaningful-access limits. Rufo retains its independent significant-change and tailored-modification rule, not an extra statutory prerequisite. Morgan Stanley and Plaut retain their limited completed-dismissal reinstatement holdings; Robertson, Klein and Wheeling Bridge preserve the changed-law/adjudication distinction. Bell preserves pretrial protection. Beach, Heller and Romer supply ordinary review within their actual limits, and Atchison supplies the assumed federal-nonparty contract analysis. No precedent is overruled.

### Service of process in suits against the United States

#### Henderson v. United States, 517 U.S. 654

**Docket or dockets:** No. 95-232.
**Decided:** May 20, 1996.

##### The SAA forthwith-service timetable is procedural, not a jurisdictional consent condition

**Holding:** Section 742's direction to serve the filed complaint forthwith regulates procedure in an already authorized Suits in Admiralty Act action; it does not independently condition consent to suit or remove subject-matter jurisdiction. Congress can make procedure a jurisdictional consent condition, but this timetable's placement, function and surrounding provisions establish that it did not do so here.

**Proposition-level authority:** Scalia's Opinion of the Court, Parts I–III, joined throughout by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; the same seven Justices adopt all three Henderson holdings. O'Connor and Thomas dissent.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Section 743's private-party practice direction supports classification without erasing its other prescriptions. Section 745's two-year commencement limit, substantive consent limits and designated service recipients remain. Neither proximity to a waiver nor procedural subject matter alone determines jurisdictional effect.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Nordic Village retains clear consent to the actual monetary remedy and distinguishes consent from general jurisdiction; it does not classify this service timetable. McNeil's prefiling administrative-exhaustion sequence and Keene's filing-time bar are distinguished from this postfiling event. Carlisle supplies the procedural-authority/jurisdiction distinction without categorically classifying all procedural commands.

##### Congress's later Rule 4 enactment displaces the incompatible service timetable

**Holding:** In a timely commenced domestic SAA action, the applicable Rule 4 timing scheme, including authorized enlargement, governs service; §742 cannot independently require dismissal for failure to serve sooner. Congress's direct enactment of former Rule 4(j) displaces the incompatible procedural timetable without enlarging substantive consent or dispensing with the designated-recipient requirements.

**Proposition-level authority:** Scalia's Part II, the same seven Justices.

**Material application:** Former Rule 4(j), directly enacted in Pub. L. 97-462, required dismissal without prejudice for failure to serve within 120 days without good cause, on motion or the court's initiative after notice, except foreign service under former subdivision (i). A separately fatal shorter timetable would deny that scheme's service allowance and authorized enlargement; the possibility of prompt compliance with both texts does not eliminate the conflict.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Section 2072 supplies a procedural/substantive framework, not an independent direct-nullification ground through a rule Congress itself enacted. Rule 82's jurisdictional limit is preserved. No deliberate disregard of service responsibilities is licensed; no universal repeal of special service statutes, government/private procedural differences or registered-versus-certified-mail requirement is decided.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Hanna and Mississippi Publishing Corp. v. Murphree support service's procedural role without replacing the actual-conflict inquiry. Walker and Ragan retain a state-created right's distinct state-law commencement condition; unlike Rule 3 there, the rival provisions here address the same service event.

##### Removing the statutory dismissal does not validate an extension or compel a new service hearing

**Holding:** The statutory dismissal must be reversed as to both designated recipients, with the governing Federal Rules applied to genuinely available, properly presented service questions in further proceedings. Any necessary use of amended Rule 4 must honor its express application to proceedings in cases pending on December 1, 1993 only insofar as just and practicable; this judgment neither validates the existing extension nor orders a new service hearing.

**Proposition-level authority:** Scalia's Part III, the same seven Justices.

**Material application:** The action was timely commenced. Attorney General receipt on day 47 and United States Attorney service on day 148 cannot sustain the displaced §742 dismissal. The latter service was outside the original 120 days but within the district court's fifteen-day direction; absence of express good-cause findings neither invalidates that order by itself nor requires renewed factfinding. No distinct Rule 4 ground supported the judgment reviewed.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Former Rule 4(j) governed the April–September 1993 acts. Amended Rule 4(m), if applicable under the transition, requires dismissal without prejudice or a direction to serve within a specified time after notice when service exceeds 120 days; good cause requires an appropriate extension, while enlargement without good cause is permitted, not compelled. Foreign service under subdivisions (f) and (j)(1) is excepted. A limitations bar may inform discretion but does not require enlargement. No Clarification Act/Public Vessels Act classification is decided. No Rule 12 waiver ground is adopted because the transfer motion's legal effect and appellate preservation are unestablished. Section 745's narrowly dated 1950 savings provision creates no general new refiling opportunity.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Reverse and remand, 7–2, for ordinary further proceedings. No new service objection, mandatory good-cause hearing, immediate trial, injury finding, maintenance or cure award, damages judgment or separate due-process ruling follows.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Pioneer preserves flexibility authorized by the particular rule, not general SAA tolling or a substitute good-cause test. Landgraf requires attention to express transition and does not automatically reopen completed acts merely because a case is pending or a provision procedural.

### Successive habeas petitions and original jurisdiction

#### Felker v. Turpin, 518 U.S. 651 (1996)

**Docket or dockets:** No. 95-8836; associated application A-890.
**Decided:** June 28, 1996.

##### Whether §2244(b)(3)(E) bars review of circuit authorization while preserving original habeas

**Holding:** Section 2244(b)(3)(E) bars ordinary certiorari review of a court of appeals' grant or denial of authorization to file a second or successive district-court habeas application; the present certiorari request must be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. The provision does not repeal the distinct original habeas authority retained by §2241, which permits independent consideration of this petition without affirming or reviewing the circuit's authorization judgment.

**Proposition-level authority:** O’Connor’s Part I-A, unanimous.

**Material application:** Section 2241 still names the Court and its Justices; §2244(b)(3)(A) concerns advance authorization for district filing, and the amended transfer rule does not name this Court. Direct filing is procedurally original but constitutionally appellate; §1651 aids existing jurisdiction rather than creates it.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Unpresented certification, interlocutory and supervisory channels are not decided.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Ordinary certiorari dismissed for want of jurisdiction, 9–0, without affirming the authorization judgment.

##### When the new authorization-review bar governs

**Holding:** The authorization and review proceedings begun after AEDPA's April 24, 1996 enactment are governed by its specified authorization-review bar. That conclusion does not decide the temporal reach of every Title I provision or apply a new substantive restriction backward merely because a petition is pending.

**Proposition-level authority:** All nine support the channel result; O’Connor’s Part I-B has Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer, six. Thomas, Scalia and Kennedy use a distinct relevant-activity approach.

**Material application:** Landgraf’s provision-specific temporal sequence governs the majority reasoning; a procedural/jurisdictional label alone does not answer retroactivity. The May authorization and subsequent review proceedings began after April 24.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No holding determines every Title I provision’s temporal reach or Georgia’s chapter 154 qualification. Chapter 154’s express pending-case direction does not automatically govern other amendments.

##### What successive restrictions and discretionary conditions govern an original petition

**Holding:** The district-court authorization mechanism does not govern filing this original application. Sections 2244(b)(1)–(2) inform the Court's consideration of repeated applications, but whether those substantive provisions bind this Court directly is reserved. Retained jurisdiction does not itself entitle an applicant to an original writ.

**Proposition-level authority:** O’Connor’s opinion, Part II, unanimous.

**Material application:** For statutory second/successive §2254 applications, (b)(1) dismisses previously presented claims. New claims under (b)(2) require either a previously unavailable new constitutional rule made retroactive by this Court, or both previously undiscoverable facts despite due diligence and facts which, if proved with the whole evidence, clearly and convincingly establish that but for constitutional error no reasonable factfinder would find guilt. A request to announce a new rule is not the first exception. Before district filing, (b)(3) requires circuit permission by a three-judge panel upon prima facie showing within thirty days; the determination permits no appeal, rehearing or certiorari. Under (b)(4), district dismissal is required unless the applicant actually establishes the conditions, despite authorization.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Whether (b)(1)–(2) bind this Court directly remains reserved; they inform the Court’s consideration. Rule 20 separately requires reasons for bypassing district court, exhaustion or satisfaction of §2254(b), exceptional circumstances and unavailability of adequate relief in another form or court. Section 2254(b)(1) permits exhaustion, absence of available state corrective process or circumstances rendering it ineffective; (b)(2) permits, but does not require, denial on merits despite nonexhaustion; counsel’s express waiver is necessary under (b)(3). No exhaustion, process adequacy, waiver or affirmative diligence-failure fact is decided.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Original relief denied, 9–0, on the exceptional-original-showing ground; no return, transfer or hearing is ordered.

##### Whether the channel and successive scheme suspend meaningful review or dictate an unlawful outcome here

**Holding:** The specified review restriction and consideration of the operative successive scheme do not suspend constitutionally sufficient habeas review or prescribe a forbidden judicial outcome as applied to these claims. The original petition receives independent examination and fails on an adequate traditional original-writ ground, without deciding that every future statutory exclusion or every nominal surviving remedy is constitutional.

**Proposition-level authority:** O’Connor’s opinion, Part II, unanimous.

**Material application:** The retained original route supplies actual independent claim examination and a sufficient traditional denial ground. Klein distinguishes changed law from a command to falsify facts or decide an unchanged rule in a prescribed manner.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No approval of every nominal forum, future exclusion of otherwise sufficient innocence claims, all AEDPA, §§2254(d)–(e), or unpresented supervisory restriction.

##### Whether the submitted medical evidence establishes the Schlup gateway

**Holding:** This submission does not establish Schlup's gateway: reliable new evidence, assessed with all probative evidence, making it more likely than not that no reasonable, properly instructed juror would convict. That conclusion does not adjudicate the separately pleaded constitutional innocence theory or make the gateway and AEDPA's successive conditions interchangeable.

**Proposition-level authority:** O’Connor’s Part IV-A, all eight Associates; Stone-Zsela withholds this additional application.

**Material application:** Detailed new three-to-five-day estimates and physiological criticisms are considered with Whitaker’s independently favored earlier death estimate, his acknowledgment that the later interval was possible, and the disappearance, car, call and clothing evidence. The submission does not eliminate reasonable adverse assessment at Schlup’s probability threshold. No affidavit is declared false and other-offense evidence retains its motive/intent/state-of-mind limit.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Gateway passage would permit consideration of a trial claim, not prove it, establish statutory (b)(2)(B), or decide a distinct constitutional innocence entitlement.

##### Whether the separately pleaded constitutional innocence claim warrants exceptional original relief

**Independent alternative holding:** Even assuming a possible constitutional claim based on actual innocence, this considered submission does not establish exceptional circumstances warranting the Court's original habeas intervention. Original relief is denied without establishing a universal freestanding-innocence burden, rejecting every such constitutional claim, or requiring an additional return merely because new expert opinions are offered.

**Proposition-level authority for alternative holding:** O’Connor’s Part IV-B, unanimous; independently sufficient original-writ ground.

**Material application:** Herrera supplies a particular-submission insufficiency holding, not one general constitutional innocence burden. The full medical dispute receives consideration; the conviction and circuit refusal alone do not replace examination.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No universal freestanding-innocence threshold, categorical denial of every such right, presumed adequate Georgia remedy or mandatory further return from new expert opinions.

##### Whether A-890 warrants protection after claim-specific consideration is complete

**Holding:** Execution's irreversibility does not alone establish entitlement to a stay. Because the independently considered claims show no sufficiently substantial basis for relief through the available proceedings and no identified unfinished legally required process warrants protection, application A-890 is denied.

**Proposition-level authority:** O’Connor’s Part V, unanimous, in the reasoned combined threshold decision.

**Material application:** Bowersox’s substantial-ground assessment remains distinct from Lonchar’s protection of legally required process and McFarland’s counsel/preparation predicates. Neither the petition’s existence nor retained jurisdiction supplies relief by itself.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No automatic lateness penalty, execution date, altered prior stay, exhaustion of all other possible avenues or execution legality determination.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The pending stay request is denied, 9–0, after independent examination; no unfinished identified required process or sufficiently substantial relief basis remains.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- **Ex parte McCardle:** Applied to the specified withdrawn appellate route; no conclusion follows that every separate habeas source is repealed.
- **Ex parte Yerger and Ex parte Bollman:** Applied to the retained statutory habeas channel and its constitutional appellate character. They do not make issuance of an original writ automatic.
- **Landgraf and Rivers:** Their controlling provision-specific temporal inquiry remains in force; the application here concerns post-enactment authorization/review proceedings, not all pending habeas litigation.
- **McCleskey v. Zant:** Its recognition of lawful successive/abuse restrictions supports consideration of the new standards; it does not eliminate their separate textual requirements or settle their mandatory reach here.
- **United States v. Klein:** Its jurisdiction/rule-of-decision distinction is preserved; the present channel and standards do not direct a factual result under unchanged law.
- **Victor and Sandoval:** The whole-charge reasonable-likelihood test is applied by the eight Associates, with its existing limits on isolated terminology and automatic cures intact.
- **Sullivan:** Its structural-error rule is preserved; the Court finds no constitutional vitiation of the proof standard and conducts no harmless-error substitute.
- **Lisenba:** Its fundamental-fairness inquiry governs the presented medical-testimony trial claim. **Ake, Ford and Eddings** do not supply the proposed automatic physician-only testimony requirement.
- **Schlup:** Its gateway remains distinct from a substantive innocence claim and the new statutory conditions; the eight Associates find the present showing insufficient under its governing probability standard.
- **Herrera:** Its particular-submission holding is preserved without converting any separate theory into a general Court rule. The present original denial likewise assumes the possible constitutional claim without deciding its universal merits threshold.
- **Bowersox, Lonchar and McFarland:** Their distinct substantial-ground, required-process and counsel/preparation rules retain their actual triggers. None guarantees additional proceedings or a stay from filing alone.

### Accepted rehearing and certiorari finality

#### Young v. Harper

**Docket or dockets:** No. 95-1598.
**Decided:** March 18, 1997.

##### Whether an expressly accepted late rehearing filing makes the subsequent certiorari petition timely

**Holding:** When the appellate court grants leave for a late rehearing filing, treats it as timely and keeps the proceeding open until disposition, denial of that accepted rehearing supplies the relevant finality point for certiorari. The petition filed within ninety days of denial on this sequence is timely.

**Proposition-level authority:** Opinion of the Court (Breyer), Part I, joined by Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; eight direct joins. Stone-Zsela agrees with the timely-review resolution without adopting its reasons.

**Limits and questions not reached:** An unauthorized late paper, an en banc suggestion not treated as rehearing, the mandate date by itself, or an order solely extending the Supreme Court filing period does not establish the same result. No statutory period is waived.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** The operative Rule 13.3 and FRAP 40 permit this accepted-rehearing sequence. Bowman distinguishes permitted and entertained rehearing from unauthorized submission; Missouri v. Jenkins, 495 U.S. 33 (1990), respects actual rehearing treatment within the statutory limit.

For the conditional-community-liberty, revocation-process and remedy holdings in Young v. Harper, No. 95-1598, decided March 18, 1997, see Criminal Procedure, “Conditional community release and revocation.”

### Class certification and extraordinary review

#### In re Rhone-Poulenc Rorer

**Docket or dockets:** Seventh Circuit No. 94-3912.
**Decided:** February 26, 1997.

##### Whether this revisable issue-certification plan warrants mandamus

**Holding:** Mandamus requires a clear and indisputable right, inadequate ordinary means of relief and circumstances justifying extraordinary intervention. Possible serious certification error, aggregate exposure and ordinary settlement pressure do not establish entitlement where arrangements remain revisable, final-judgment review is available and no otherwise-unavoidable jury deprivation has been demonstrated.

**Proposition-level authority:** Opinion of the Court (Stone-Zsela), unanimous; all nine Justices join both holdings.

**Material application:** The appellate court assumed eventual review after named-plaintiff final judgment. There was no common verdict or fixed sequence making jury reexamination unavoidable; earlier defense verdicts did not decide the remaining claims.

**Limits and questions not reached:** A litigant need not first endure an established, otherwise-unavoidable deprivation of jury rights. The holding creates neither class-action immunity from mandamus nor an immediate-review entitlement based on litigation stakes.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The mandamus judgment is reversed with directions to deny this petition, removing the appellate decertification command. The Court does not certify a class or approve a trial plan.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Kerr, Allied Chemical and Mallard preserve the extraordinary-writ conditions; In re Blodgett requires examination of actual ordinary remedies. Coopers & Lybrand, Digital Equipment and Swint preserve finality without eliminating Swint’s mandamus reservation. Beacon Theatres and Dairy Queen permit preventive protection of an established jury entitlement.

##### Which state-law, certification and jury limits survive reversal of the writ

**Holding:** Any continued issue certification must satisfy Rule 23 under the governing state laws, retain genuine defenses and protect the functions of each jury. Material legal equivalence, lawful grouping or genuine issue separability must be demonstrated; convenience cannot replace state negligence law with an averaged national rule or authorize a later jury to redecide facts assigned to the first.

**Proposition-level authority:** Opinion of the Court (Stone-Zsela), unanimous.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court decides neither negligence nor the relationship between action-wide predominance and issue certification reserved in Castano. No replacement instructions, preclusion ruling, damages or stay are supplied.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The District Court retains its ordinary responsibility to reconsider certification and trial arrangements within these limits.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Castano requires a concrete law-and-proof showing, without categorical tort-maturation or settlement-pressure barriers. Erie, Klaxon and O’Melveny preserve governing state law; Gasperini preserves substantive rules and lawful federal allocation without supplying a class-trial formula. Gasoline Products requires separability for successive juries. Matsushita and Richards independently require adequate representation and lawful authority to bind absent persons.

### Class certification and multistate claims

#### Castano v. American Tobacco Co.

**Docket or dockets:** Fifth Circuit No. 95-30725.
**Decided:** January 14, 1997.

##### Certification requires a demonstrated legal and evidentiary basis

**Holding:** Before certifying a Rule 23(b)(3) class, a court must determine from the actual claims, governing law and anticipated proof that common questions predominate and class adjudication is superior to the available alternatives, together with satisfaction of Rule 23(a). Conditional certification does not permit postponing that showing, and a claim's novelty neither dispenses with rigorous analysis nor categorically bars certification until individual verdicts exist.

**Proposition-level authority:** Opinion of the Court (Ginsburg), unanimous.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The inquiry may examine merits-linked elements needed to assess certification but may not award or deny certification simply by predicting success. No prior-verdict quota, automatic exclusion of novel torts or mandatory separately titled trial-plan document is required.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Falcon supplies rigorous examination; Eisen bars certification based merely on a preliminary merits prediction, without limiting certification to the pleadings. Matsushita and Richards preserve adequate representation and the lawful basis for binding absent persons without establishing this class's adequacy.

##### The present core-liability class cannot stand

**Holding:** This nationwide core-liability certification fails Rule 23(b)(3) because the court deferred the material state-law inquiry and did not show how common issues, individual addiction, reliance, causation and defenses would fit into lawful, manageable adjudication. Differences among state laws do not automatically prohibit every multistate class, but proponents must demonstrate materially common answers or workable groupings rather than assume uniformity or rely on subclass labels.

**Proposition-level authority:** Opinion of the Court (Ginsburg), unanimous.

**Material application:** The certification separated common manufacturer conduct from injury, causation, reliance, defenses and compensatory damages without demonstrating how their legally varied resolution could work together.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not determine governing state law or settle the full relationship between Rule 23(b)(3) and issue certification under (c)(4), including action-wide predominance. State-law variation alone does not prohibit every national class.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Shutts forbids assuming one State's law for materially disconnected claims; it does not supply the choice-of-law result here.

##### The punitive component and superiority finding also fail

**Holding:** The certified punitive-ratio component fails because its state-law predicates, burdens, relation to liability and coordination with individual proceedings were not demonstrated; those same gaps defeat the present superiority finding. Settlement pressure from a procedure that bypasses defenses or detaches punitive assessment from established claims may reinforce concrete certification defects, but aggregate size or ordinary settlement pressure alone is not a categorical bar.

**Proposition-level authority:** Opinion of the Court (Ginsburg), unanimous.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The ruling establishes no new Seventh Amendment rule or general prohibition of punitive ratios, issue classes or bifurcation. It resolves no individual liability, damages, Article III severance or complete Erie objection. The proposed Liggett settlement establishes no completed release or mootness.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Decertification of the existing core-liability and punitive components is affirmed, but the mandate requiring dismissal and foreclosing reconsideration because the tort has not matured is vacated. Individual litigation or a materially narrower supported class proposal may proceed under all applicable Rule 23 requirements, without a certification presumption, discovery entitlement or deadline. The unappealed Rule 23(b)(2) equitable/medical-monitoring denial is not reopened.

### Finality and conditional summons enforcement

#### United States v. Jose

**Docket or dockets:** No. 95-2082.

**Decided:** December 2, 1996.

##### Immediate review of the completed conditional enforcement judgment

**Holding:** An order completing a summons-enforcement proceeding is final under 28 U.S.C. §1291, including its presently binding notice condition. The Government's challenge to this condition is ripe before an interdivision transfer occurs because the judgment already fixes its legal obligation; it need not violate the order or await contempt to obtain review.

**Proposition-level authority:** Per curiam opinion, unanimous.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The remand concerns the notice condition's legality and preserved related enforcement-power issues. The uncontested findings that the civil-purpose summonses are valid and should be enforced are not reopened. Privacy interests and hypothetical future criminal uses are not adjudicated by this threshold ruling. Zolin's equal division supplies no controlling answer about conditions.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Church of Scientology distinguishes meaningful appellate relief from merits entitlement. Digital Equipment and Quackenbush retain source-specific appellate routes and collateral-order limits; this completed proceeding uses ordinary finality. Zolin's equal division supplies no controlling condition-authority rule.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Reverse the ripeness dismissal and remand for review of the preserved notice-condition challenge covering both summonses; uncontested enforcement validity remains closed.

### Immigration review transition

#### INS v. Yueh-Shaio Yang

**Docket or dockets:** No. 95-938.

**Decided:** November 13, 1996.

For the other questions in INS v. Yueh-Shaio Yang, No. 95-938, decided November 13, 1996, see Immigration - Discretionary relief from entry fraud (Eligibility does not exclude the continuing fraud pattern from discretion; Permissible factors remain subject to reasoned and consistent administration).

##### Review under the corrected 1996 transition provisions

**Holding:** Review of this existing deportation proceeding remains available under former INA §106 and 28 U.S.C. §1254(1) on November 13, 1996. Corrected IIRIRA §306(c)(1) gives new §242(g) reach across past, pending and future proceedings when that provision commences; it does not advance commencement of the new jurisdictional rule from April 1, 1997, and the other review restrictions establish no present bar on this record.

**Proposition-level authority:** Souter's Part I, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer; eight Justices. Stone-Zsela agrees only with the threshold resolution.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No new qualifying final order, election under section 309(c)(2) or (3), or covered criminal conviction is established. Section 306(c)(2) protects existing section 106 judgments from invalidation or compelled reconsideration but independently confers no jurisdiction. Section 242(g)'s postcommencement scope remains open.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Landgraf and Rivers require attention to enacted temporal directions; their different earlier rationales are not merged. The Court construes the corrected IIRIRA timing text itself.

**Later-authority backlinks:** Reyes-Hernandez v. INS, May 12, 1997, resolves §242(g)'s reserved post-April 1 scope for these legal challenges to completed adjudication, preserving the otherwise saved former §106 route outside the three enumerated executive actions.

#### Reyes-Hernandez v. INS

**Docket or dockets:** Seventh Circuit No. 95-3677; Supreme Court docket unassigned.
**Decided:** 1997-05-12.

For discretionary denial and the new-evidence vehicle, see Immigration — Waiver discretion and supplementary evidence, Reyes-Hernandez, May 12, 1997, this docket.

##### Section 242(g) does not withdraw review of these completed-adjudication claims

**Holding:** After its April 1, 1997 commencement, §242(g) reaches past, pending and future proceedings but withdraws review of the identified executive decisions or actions to commence proceedings, adjudicate cases or execute removal orders, rather than every legal challenge arising from completed adjudication. These challenges to temporal eligibility, the legality of the completed waiver denial and treatment of a supplemental brief remain outside that withdrawal and may use the otherwise saved former §106 review route.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stevens's Part I, joined by all seven other Associates; eight rationale votes. Stone-Zsela agrees only in the threshold result.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Corrected §309(c)(1) saves earlier proceedings subject to specific transitions: paragraph (2) allows election only before the evidentiary hearing begins, on thirty days' notice; paragraph (3) allows termination/reinitiation only before a final administrative decision. Neither condition exists after the completed 1995 adjudication. The October 1995 order is not an order entered more than thirty days after September 30, 1996 under paragraph (4). Section 306(c)(2) protects existing §106 judgments but confers no jurisdiction. No election, later qualifying order, general constitutional-review entitlement or alternative habeas basis is found.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Yang's April 1 commencement rule is applied and its reserved postcommencement scope resolved at this boundary; the admitted corrected §§306 and 309 retain their different timing and transition commands. Felker requires identifying the channel actually withdrawn or retained; hypothetical §2241 or §1651 remedies supply no jurisdiction here.

##### The two AEDPA restrictions do not attach these new consequences to the completed concession

**Holding:** On the uncontested premise that Reyes surrendered a colorable defense to deportability before enactment in order to pursue the then-available waiver-and-review path, §440(d) does not remove eligibility for that original waiver claim, and §440(a) does not eliminate ordinary review of its lawful denial, because neither clearly prescribes those new consequences for that completed choice. A genuine defense is necessary to this lost-option rationale, not a universal element of retroactivity analysis or an exemption for every preenactment conviction, pending case or later reopening request.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stevens's Parts II–IV, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; six direct joins. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas would dismiss under §440(a) and supply no merits votes.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Section 440(f) addresses subsection (e), not (a) or (d). A lost colorable defense is necessary for this surrendered-option rationale, not a universal retroactivity element or subjective-reliance requirement. No particular defense is invented; the Government accepted the premise. Other temporal predicates, later reopening requests, constitutional invalidation and habeas remain open.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Landgraf requires separate examination of enacted direction and the consequences of each provision; a jurisdictional label or mere pendency does not decide retroactivity. Felker's post-enactment authorization proceedings differ.

#### Hincapie-Nieto v. INS

**Docket or dockets:** Second Circuit No. 96-4022; no separate Supreme Court docket supplied.
**Decided:** May 27, 1997.

##### The saved procedural route remains subject to AEDPA's separate review restriction

**Holding:** IIRIRA §309(c)(1), as corrected, preserves the former procedure for proceedings begun before April 1, 1997, subject to its exceptions; corrected §306(c)(1) nevertheless gives §242(g) reach across past, pending and future proceedings after that commencement. Under Reyes-Hernandez, this review of a completed adjudication does not challenge the identified executive decision or action to commence proceedings, adjudicate cases or execute an order, so §242(g) does not itself withdraw the saved route; another applicable statute still may.

**Proposition-level authority:** Opinion of the Court (O'Connor), Part I, all eight Associate Justices; Stone-Zsela concurs in the judgment only.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The January 18, 1996 final order does not meet corrected §309(c)(4)'s trigger of a final order entered more than thirty days after September 30, 1996. Paragraph (2) requires an evidentiary hearing not yet begun and notice at least thirty days before it; paragraph (3) requires no final administrative decision. No qualifying election exists here. Section 306(c)(2) protects existing §106 judgments and orders from invalidation or required reconsideration under paragraph (1), but creates no jurisdiction. The permanent scheme does not govern wholesale merely because the Court acts after April 1.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Yang and Reyes-Hernandez are applied to the distinct transition provisions and §242(g)'s limited subject matter.

##### Section 440(a) reaches this pending petition without a proved completed-event disability

**Holding:** Section 440(a) withdraws ordinary appellate review of this final order based on admitted drug and aggravated-felony grounds even assuming the February 16 filing date. Under Landgraf, the change in future reviewing authority does not on this record attach a new legal disability to an identified completed surrender of a real defense or other protected completed event; filing and expectation of review alone do not establish that disability.

**Proposition-level authority:** O'Connor's Part II, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; six direct joins. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas accept the result on a distinct future-review rationale.

**Material application:** Deportability on drug and aggravated-felony grounds was admitted, and the agency considered discretionary relief before §440(d). No surrendered colorable defense is identified; the February 16 filing date is assumed in the petitioner's favor.

**Limits and questions not reached:** A jurisdictional label alone does not resolve temporal reach, and surrender of a defense is not the only conceivable completed-event predicate. Section 440(f) addresses subsection (e), not a saving rule for (a). Section 306(d)'s correction operates as if part of AEDPA and preserves the dual-offense branch's requirement that both predicates are otherwise covered regardless of commission dates; that branch does not decide this case. Section 440(d)'s eligibility withdrawal is not decided.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Landgraf and Rivers supply provision-specific temporal and completed-consequence analysis. Reyes-Hernandez is distinguished because its protected lost-defense predicate is absent; its reservation of other completed-event predicates remains.

##### The channel-specific dismissal does not adjudicate unpresented collateral protection

**Holding:** This record does not require retention of the particular ordinary appellate channel for further review of the denial of discretion. The Court's affirmance neither holds that all meaningful review of an actually presented constitutional or legal defect may be eliminated nor decides whether §2241 supplies review of a deportation order's legal basis.

**Proposition-level authority:** Opinion of the Court (O'Connor), Part III, all eight Associate Justices; Stone-Zsela's affirmative §2241 construction is not controlling.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Government's concession of possible detention review establishes neither review of the deportation order's legal basis nor an adequate substitute. Custody, respondent, forum, exhaustion, the nature of constitutionally required review and §2241's availability remain undecided. No unfiled petition is converted or transferred, and §1651 creates no independent jurisdiction.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Felker involved an actual retained original application receiving independent consideration, not a hypothetical substitute. Flores preserves its own custody safeguards without settling these collateral-review questions.

**Later-authority backlinks:** Kolster v. INS, First Circuit No. 96-1194, 1997-06-23, resolves retained §2241 capability for substantial legal and constitutional objections, including legal pretermission of discretionary-relief eligibility, subject to actual habeas predicates; see Federal Courts — Immigration review channels and statutory habeas.

##### Affirmance dismisses ordinary review without approving the discretionary merits

**Holding:** The direct-review dismissal is affirmed without reaching the agency's alternative merits defense or deciding an unfiled collateral claim. No new waiver hearing, reopening, stay or execution direction follows, and no assumed custody date, later final order or unproved timeliness defect supplies the judgment.

**Proposition-level authority:** Opinion of the Court (O'Connor), Part IV, unanimous.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The ordinary petition remains dismissed for lack of jurisdiction; the agency's alternative merits defense is not reached.

#### Salazar-Haro v. INS

**Docket or dockets:** Third Circuit No. 96-3007.
**Decided:** June 16, 1997.

##### The saved immigration proceeding remains subject to AEDPA’s separate bar and the actual-judgment protection

**Holding:** The saved former procedure governs this old deportation proceeding, subject to applicable transition exceptions, while §242(g)'s cross-temporal reach does not itself withdraw review of the completed-adjudication claims presented here. That conclusion preserves no exemption from AEDPA §440(a), whose separate temporal operation must be decided. Section 306(c)(2) preserves an actual judicial judgment or order entered under former INA §106 (8 U.S.C. §1105a), applying §106 as amended by AEDPA §440, against an asserted operation of §306(c)(1) that would invalidate that judgment or order or require its reconsideration. The Third Circuit's September 13, 1996 dismissal falls within that protection, which neither independently confers jurisdiction nor reopens merits review nor bars ordinary appellate review of the judgment's correctness under applicable law.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part I of Breyer's opinion, adopted by all eight Associate Justices; Stone-Zsela agrees only with the transition disposition.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Corrected §309(c)(1) saves proceedings begun before April 1, 1997, subject to its exceptions. Paragraph (2) permits election of new procedures only before the evidentiary hearing begins, with notice at least thirty days before it; paragraph (3) permits termination and reinitiation only before a final administrative decision. No qualifying election is established. Section 309(c)(4) requires a final exclusion or deportation order entered more than thirty days after September 30, 1996; this earlier order does not qualify. Section 242(g) retains its special cross-temporal operation over commencing proceedings, adjudicating cases and executing orders, but does not itself bar these completed-adjudication claims.

**Material application:** The September 13, 1996 judicial dismissal applied former INA §106 as amended by AEDPA §440(a). Section 306(c)(2) protects that actual judgment from invalidation or required reconsideration attributable to §306(c)(1), without insulating its correctness from ordinary appellate review. Public Law 104-302 made §306(c)(1) subject to §309 with September 30 effect and left paragraph (2) unchanged.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Yang supplies commencement; Reyes-Hernandez and Hincapie-Nieto supply the corrected transition construction and the distinction between specified executive action and completed legal adjudication. Their savings do not nullify AEDPA’s independent restriction.

##### Section 440(a) withdraws this pending direct-review channel without a new disability attached to a protected completed event

**Holding:** AEDPA §440(a) applies to this qualifying final deportation order despite the January 17, 1996 petition because withdrawal of future ordinary appellate review attaches no new legal disability to a protected completed event established by this record. Filing, prior conviction, family hardship and an expectation of favorable review alone establish no such disability; the agency had already considered discretionary waiver under the former law.

**Proposition-level authority:** Breyer's Part II, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter and Ginsburg: six Justices.

**Limits and questions not reached:** A surrendered colorable defense is one possible protected completed-event predicate, not a universal prerequisite. Section 440(f) concerns subsection (e), not a saving clause for subsection (a). The agency considered waiver under the former law; the separate operation of §440(d) eligibility restrictions is not decided. Pendency alone gives no blanket exemption, and a jurisdictional label gives no categorical answer.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Affirm the jurisdictional dismissal, unanimously as to that disposition, without adopting the Third Circuit’s hypothetical merits footnote. No waiver, reopening, new hearing, transfer, stay or execution direction follows.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Landgraf and Rivers require a provision-specific completed-event inquiry. Hincapie-Nieto controls the absence of a protected choice based only on filing and expectation; Reyes-Hernandez is distinguished on its actual surrendered-defense predicate.

##### The discretionary-balance record does not decide the availability of an unfiled collateral action

**Holding:** This record does not require preservation of ordinary appellate review for another weighing of discretionary equities, and a constitutional label or §1651 alone does not restore that jurisdiction. Affirmance neither approves eliminating every meaningful judicial forum for an actually presented legal or constitutional defect nor decides the availability, scope or custody, respondent, forum, exhaustion and other predicates of immigration review under §2241.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part III of Breyer's opinion, adopted in full by all eight Associate Justices; Stone-Zsela additionally joins the conclusion that this record presents no distinct legal defect requiring discretionary reweighing.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No custody status, collateral filing, adequate substitute or satisfaction of statutory predicates is presumed. The holding neither recognizes affirmative immigration §2241 jurisdiction nor declares every meaningful forum closed.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Felker concerned an actual retained original channel, not an assumed immigration substitute. Flores preserves its custody and facial-review safeguards without deciding this collateral issue. The Japanese Immigrant Case supplies antecedent due process, not a right to judicial reweighing of every waiver denial. McCardle, Yerger and Heikkila retain their channel-specific significance. Section 1651 assists jurisdiction already present; it does not create it.

**Later-authority backlinks:** Kolster v. INS, June 23, 1997, First Circuit No. 96-1194, resolves the retained §2241 route for substantial legal and constitutional objections when its actual jurisdictional and procedural predicates are satisfied, including a developed legal-eligibility objection. It does not authorize reweighing discretionary equities.

### Law-of-nations jurisdiction and political questions

#### Abebe-Jira v. Negewo

**Docket or dockets:** No. 95-8873; Eleventh Circuit No. 93-9133.

**Decided:** January 14, 1997.

For the other questions in Abebe-Jira v. Negewo, No. 95-8873; Eleventh Circuit No. 93-9133, decided January 14, 1997, see Civil Rights - Civil actions for personal official torture (A confined received action for personally committed official torture; Compensation for proved injury within that action; Punitive authority requires an independently justified aggravated-tort remedy).

##### Jurisdiction does not itself establish a damages action

**Holding:** Section 1350 supplies district-court jurisdiction over an alien's civil tort action alleging a violation of the law of nations or a United States treaty; these substantial allegations of official torture fall within that jurisdiction. Jurisdiction alone neither supplies a domestic damages action nor establishes liability, sovereign-immunity waiver or authority for every asserted international claim.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stevens's Part I, unanimous.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No sovereign-immunity issue is decided and jurisdiction does not establish liability.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Suter's source/action distinction and Meyer's separation of jurisdiction, consent and substantive liability are preserved; neither previously decided §1350's present application.

##### The foreign setting does not make this individual tort a political question

**Holding:** Adjudication of these individual official-torture claims is not categorically barred as a political question because it applies a determinate prohibition to personal conduct without deciding the legitimacy of Ethiopia's government, directing United States diplomacy or resolving a constitutionally committed war-powers dispute. A concrete immunity defense or contrary political-branch determination would require its own consideration; none is supplied or decided here.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stevens's Part V, unanimous; the jurisdictional and political-question agreements of Scalia and Thomas do not establish agreement on the action or damages.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The conclusion does not decide an immunity defense or establish the independent cause of action and remedies.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Baker's issue-specific inquiry, as retained in Montana and Nixon, is applied. Sanchez-Espinoza is distinguished at its domestic-immunity and United States foreign-policy setting; its result is not extended to this defendant.

#### Kadic v. Karadzic; Doe v. Karadzic

**Docket or dockets:** Second Circuit Nos. 94-9035 and 94-9069.
**Decided:** 1997-04-21.
