### Original Title VII mixed-motive same-decision defense

**Governing question:** Liability under the original Price Waterhouse rule for conduct governed by pre-1991 law.

**Current rule:** Direct decisional evidence, proved by a preponderance, that protected religion was a substantial factor actually relied on shifts the burden to the employer to prove by a preponderance that it would have made the same decision without that consideration. Under the original rule, carrying that burden defeats liability, not merely relief.

**Authority by component:**

- Brown v. Polk County — Part III — The original mixed-motive defense fails on this completed record, 1997-03-17; Part III of the Court's opinion, joined by all eight Associates; Stone-Zsela agrees with resolved liability without joining these same-decision reasons

**Present operation effective:** Brown v. Polk County, 1997-03-17, for the original regime applied to pre-1991 conduct.

**Effective transition:** This entry governs the original rule applicable to pre-1991 conduct; it does not replace the distinct liabilities and remedies of the 1991 Civil Rights Act.

**Exceptions and limits:** The direct-decisional-evidence trigger and actual reliance must be established; no universal burden shift follows from a religious employment dispute. Liability and the lawful calculation and availability of relief remain distinct.

**Holdings navigation:** Brown v. Polk County (1997-03-17) — Labor and Employment / Religious accommodation and completed mixed-motive proof.

### ERISA interference with prospective welfare-plan rights

**Governing question:** Whether welfare benefits outside statutory vesting protection are covered by ERISA §510.

**Current rule:** Section 510 reaches covered discharge or other prohibited conduct undertaken to interfere with attainment of a right the participant may become entitled to under a welfare plan. Nonvesting status is no categorical defense: lawful amendment or termination of plan terms differs from prohibited conduct directed at participants. The claim still requires the applicable participant or beneficiary status, protected plan right, prohibited action, interference purpose, causation and relief authorized through §510's reference to §502.

**Authority by component:**

- Inter-Modal Rail Employees Association v. Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway Co. — I. Section 510 includes prospective welfare-plan rights, 1997-05-12; Ginsburg, all nine
- Inter-Modal Rail Employees Association v. Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway Co. — II. The categorical dismissal is vacated for the remaining statutory inquiries, 1997-05-12; eight Associates

**Present operation effective:** Inter-Modal, 1997-05-12.

**Exceptions and limits:** The decision creates no permanent-benefits or general unfair-dismissal rule. Attainment where the participant is already eligible remains unresolved.

**Holdings navigation:** Inter-Modal Rail Employees Association v. Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway Co. (1997-05-12) — Section 510 includes prospective welfare-plan rights; Inter-Modal Rail Employees Association v. Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway Co. (1997-05-12) — The categorical dismissal is vacated for the remaining statutory inquiries.

### Independent user additions under maritime economic-loss law

**Governing question:** Whether resale absorbs user-added property into the original manufacturer's product.

**Current rule:** Independent equipment added by an actual initial user after manufacturer delivery retains other-property status when a defect in the original product damages it, notwithstanding resale together with the product. The controlling rule concerns additions that did not cause the casualty. Original manufacture and initial distribution remain integrated; components cannot be separated artificially to create outside-property damage.

**Authority by component:**

- Saratoga Fishing Co. v. J.M. Martinac & Co. — I. Resale does not make independent user additions the manufacturer's product, 1997-06-02; Stevens with Stone-Zsela, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; six

**Present operation effective:** Saratoga Fishing, 1997-06-02.

**Exceptions and limits:** Causal additions, disputed provenance, replacements and mixed user/assembler arrangements remain unresolved. Separate causation, comparative fault, supported loss and valid contractual risk allocations remain necessary; resale alone establishes neither waiver nor recovery.

**Holdings navigation:** Saratoga Fishing Co. v. J. M. Martinac & Co. (1997-06-02) — Maritime Law / Products liability and user-added property.

### Military statement-based conduct inference and evidentiary use

**Governing question:** The §654(b)(2) statement route, construed as a rebuttable conduct-related military personnel inference.

**Current rule:** Under ordinary rational-basis review, a voluntary declaration of homosexual or bisexual identity may be treated as rebuttable evidence of prohibited acts, propensity or intent where propensity means likelihood of acts beyond abstract preference or desire and a genuine rebuttal opportunity exists. The sustained application requires neither a completed act nor individualized operational impairment; it is not a conclusive orientation exclusion. Section 654(b)(2) directs separation after the approved statement finding unless a further approved finding establishes that the member demonstrated no engagement, attempted engagement, propensity or intent to engage in homosexual acts. The First Amendment permits the relevant evidentiary use at that conduct-related scope, without permitting punishment for abstract belief or opposition to the policy.

**Authority by component:**

- Thomasson v. Perry — I. The conduct-related, rebuttable statement inference is constitutional in this application, 1997-06-09; O'Connor with Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas and Breyer; five
- Thomasson v. Perry — II. The First Amendment permits this relevant evidentiary use of the statement, 1997-06-09; the same five

**Present operation effective:** Thomasson, 1997-06-09.

**Exceptions and limits:** Section 654(e) permits omission of processing if the military determines both intent to avoid or terminate service and that separation would not serve its best interest; it does not compel omission. The act and marriage routes have distinct predicates and are not adjudicated here. Denial of meaningful rebuttal, an irrelevant inference, an irrebuttable status exclusion or retaliation for advocacy remains distinct. Service excellence is not an automatic defense, and every identity statement is not an admission of an act. No facial validation, civilian-employment rule, new scrutiny tier or investigation checklist follows; independent due-process, APA, directive-validity and substantive-liberty claims remain undecided.

**Holdings navigation:** Thomasson v. Perry (1997-06-09) — A genuinely rebuttable conduct inference sustains this statement-based separation; Thomasson v. Perry (1997-06-09) — First Amendment / Military statements as relevant evidence.

### Title VII limits on diversity-based selection for layoff

**Governing question:** Whether voluntary affirmative action permits race to select an incumbent for discharge solely to preserve departmental diversity.

**Current rule:** A tie in qualifications and seniority does not remove a race-selected discharge from Title VII. The Weber–Johnson accommodation does not authorize such a nonremedial diversity-only layoff without a connection to a manifest imbalance in a traditionally segregated job category. A qualifying remedial plan need not rest on proof that the employer committed an actionable past violation. Constitutional permission to pursue a diversity interest does not itself supply statutory permission under Title VII.

**Authority by component:**
- Independent statutory permission: Taxman, Piscataway Township Board of Education v. Taxman — I. Statutory permission and constitutional permission remain distinct, O'Connor Part I, all nine, 1997-06-16.
- Remedial connection: Taxman, Piscataway Township Board of Education v. Taxman — II. This nonremedial layoff lies outside the recognized accommodation, O'Connor Parts II–III, joined by Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas (five), 1997-06-16.

**Present operation effective:** Taxman, 1997-06-16.

**Exceptions and limits:** This rule neither condemns every remedial layoff plan nor decides the separate constitutional question of faculty diversity. The independent unnecessary-burden holding rests on the particular loss, missing remedial limiting goal and available nonracial tie procedure; it is not a categorical prohibition on every preference that burdens another employee.

**Holdings navigation:** Piscataway Township Board of Education v. Taxman (1997-06-16) — Labor and Employment / Voluntary affirmative action and layoffs.

### Independent medical-monitoring damages under FELA

**Governing question:** Whether asymptomatic negligent asbestos exposure supports independent lump-sum medical-monitoring damages.

**Current rule:** Negligent exposure, increased future disease risk and recommended surveillance in an asymptomatic record do not establish entitlement to independent, unqualified lump-sum monitoring damages under FELA. Those damages cannot be appended to an emotional-distress claim that fails its separate injury threshold. The requirement of injury remains distinct from negligence and relaxed causation.

**Authority by component:**
- Boundary of the damages category: Metro-North v. Buckley, Metro-North Commuter Railroad Co. v. Buckley — II. FELA does not authorize the independent, unqualified monitoring damages recognized below, Thomas with O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Breyer (six), 1997-06-23.

**Present operation effective:** Metro-North v. Buckley, 1997-06-23.

**Open question:** Carefully limited monitoring programs, reimbursement of actual necessary costs, later illness and materially different records remain undecided; no universal bar on every monitoring arrangement is adopted.

**Holdings navigation:** Metro-North Commuter Railroad Co. v. Buckley (1997-06-23) — II. FELA does not authorize the independent, unqualified monitoring damages recognized below.

### Withdrawal-liability collection accrual and installments

**Governing question:** When a withdrawal-liability collection claim accrues under §1451(f).

**Current rule:** Withdrawal creates liability but collection accrues only after assessment, scheduling and demand when a due installment is not paid. Section 1451(f) allows the longer of six years after accrual or three years after actual or constructive knowledge of the cause; fraud or concealment permits suit within six years after discovery. Each missed installment has its own period. A legally effective election to accelerate starts the period for accelerated debt, but a later aggregate demand does not revive already barred installments.

**Authority by component:**

- Collection accrual; separate installments and effective acceleration: Bay Area Laundry and Dry Cleaning Pension Trust Fund v. Ferbar Corp. of California, 1997-12-15; Breyer Parts I–II for all nine Justices.

**Present operation effective:** 1997-12-15.

**Sequence or decisionmaker:** The plan must assess and demand payment as soon as practicable. Payments begin no later than sixty days after demand notwithstanding review or appeal. Payment default requires failure to cure within sixty days after written notice; another plan-defined default must indicate substantial likelihood of inability to pay. Default alone is not an election to accelerate.

**Open question:** Whether a complaint’s alternative full-debt demand itself effects acceleration remains unresolved.

**Related current rules:** Withdrawal-liability installment assumptions and separate collection triggers governs computation and payment; those computational assumptions do not establish collection accrual.

**Holdings navigation:** Bay Area Laundry and Dry Cleaning Pension Trust Fund v. Ferbar Corp. of California — Pension withdrawal-liability collection and limitations.

### Knowing false denials in federal employee discipline

**Governing question:** Whether due process or the CSRA immunizes knowing factual falsification when answering misconduct charges.

**Current rule:** The meaningful opportunity to answer does not immunize an otherwise punishable knowingly false factual denial. The agency must prove the actual falsification and culpability under governing employment rules; losing the underlying dispute, honest mistake, uncertain recollection, legal disagreement and procedural nonadmission are not themselves knowing lies. Otherwise lawful consideration of proved falsity for penalty or credibility is permitted, not mandatory. Sections 7513 and 7701 preserve the actual cause, service-efficiency, process, proof and review requirements rather than establish denial immunity.

**Authority by component:**

- Meaningful answer without denial immunity; conditional penalty and credibility use: LaChance v. Erickson / LaChance v. McManus, 1998-01-21; Souter Part I for all nine; Parts II–III for all eight Associates, with Stone-Zsela additionally joining Part III’s penalty and actual-proof/lawful-procedure qualifications.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-01-21.

**Burdens and proof:** Ordinary misconduct requires preponderance proof under §7701(c); specified performance and senior-executive matters retain their separate substantial-evidence rule. Harmful procedural error, prohibited personnel practices or legal invalidity prevent sustaining otherwise supported action. No criminal burden, jury, different-source corroboration requirement or universal materiality element is added.

**Sequence or decisionmaker:** Section 7513 ordinarily requires thirty days’ advance notice of specific reasons, except on reasonable cause to believe an imprisonable crime was committed; at least seven days to answer orally and in writing with documents or affidavits; representation; and a timely written reasoned decision. Agency hearing permission under §7513(c) is distinct from Board hearing and appeal rights. Required records remain available on request. Section 7703 review is distinct from agency proof, with designated discrimination facts receiving their own de novo treatment.

**Exceptions and limits:** Genuine compelled-incrimination claims and protection against mandatory waiver remain separate. The applicable reporting duty must satisfy its actual authorization and nondisclosure exceptions; no general duty to confess follows. Garrity’s criminal-use protection and Gardner’s official-duty/no-waiver distinction remain intact.

**Holdings navigation:** LaChance v. Erickson; LaChance v. McManus — False denials in federal employment discipline.

### Objective doubt before polling an incumbent union

**Governing question:** The prerequisite for an employer’s safeguarded poll of an incumbent union.

**Current rule:** The Board may require good-faith reasonable doubt of majority support based on objective considerations before a safeguarded poll. The same prerequisite for polling, withdrawal of recognition and requesting a Board election is not inherently irrational. Doubt means objective uncertainty rather than proof of actual minority; cumulative circumstantial evidence may suffice without a counted majority’s direct repudiations. Safeguards do not replace the prerequisite, and the permissible policy is not compulsory for every future Board.

**Authority by component:**

- Permissible reasonable-doubt polling threshold; actual doubt rather than minority proof: Allentown Mack Sales & Service, Inc. v. NLRB, 1998-01-26; Scalia Part II with Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; Parts III–IV with Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Kennedy and Thomas.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-01-26.

**Exceptions and limits:** Polling safeguards remain a truth-testing purpose communicated to employees, assurances against reprisal, a secret ballot, no unfair labor practices or coercive atmosphere, and advance time-and-place notice. Lawful certification and contract protections and statutory representation routes remain separate. No unconditional right to poll, headcount threshold or independent First Amendment rule is adopted.

**Related current rules:** Incumbent-union doubt before acceptance of a bargaining offer governs the distinct accepted-offer cutoff.

**Holdings navigation:** Allentown Mack Sales & Service, Inc. v. NLRB — Incumbent-union polling and agency evidentiary standards.

### ADEA waiver safeguards despite retention of consideration

**Governing question:** Whether retaining consideration or failing to tender it back bars an ADEA claim under a deficient waiver.

**Current rule:** A waiver failing applicable §626(f) minimum conditions cannot bar an ADEA action through retention-based ratification, prior tender or estoppel accomplishing the same bar. The party asserting validity must prove a knowing and voluntary waiver under the applicable statutory paragraph; signature, consultation and later awareness do not replace missing statutory safeguards. For an ordinary individual waiver the safeguards include understandable writing, a specific ADEA reference, no waiver of future claims, additional consideration, written advice to consult an attorney, at least twenty-one days to consider and seven days to revoke after execution.

**Authority by component:**

- Deficient waiver cannot be enforced through retention or prior tender: Oubre v. Entergy Operations, Inc., 1998-01-26; O’Connor with Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-01-26.

**Exceptions and limits:** Applicable group-program forty-five-day and disclosure requirements remain distinct. Settlement of an already filed charge or action under paragraph (2) requires paragraph (1)(A)–(E) and a reasonable consideration period. Compliant waivers remain possible; distinct fraud, contract or equitable claims, other released rights, restitution, recoupment and setoff remain unresolved. No automatic repayment or deduction follows, and the employee must prove discrimination. EEOC enforcement and participation protection under §626(f)(4) remains independent.

**Holdings navigation:** Oubre v. Entergy Operations, Inc. — Age-discrimination waivers and tender.

### Actual violation controversies under LMRA §301

**Governing question:** When does a dispute about a labor contract’s validity fall within §301(a)?

**Current rule:** Section 301(a) authorizes suits for violation of covered contracts, not every formation or validity dispute. A standalone formation-fraud action alleging no violation and presenting no actual or threatened violation controversy does not satisfy that jurisdictional gateway. Validity may be decided when necessary to a properly brought violation dispute; a declaratory action must independently establish the applicable jurisdictional and controversy requirements.

**Authority by component:**

- Violation gateway, validity-defense distinction and bounded declaratory route: Textron Lycoming Reciprocating Engine Division v. United Automobile Workers — Contract validity alone does not establish a suit for violation, 1998-05-18.

**Present operation effective:** Textron Lycoming v. United Automobile Workers, 1998-05-18.

**Related current rules:** Member enforcement of interunion contracts under §301 permits a qualifying beneficiary to enforce a covered contract but does not eliminate the violation predicate.

**Exceptions and limits:** No broad §1331 or federal-common-law jurisdiction ruling follows. Fraud, breach, validity, labor-board and State-remedy merits retain their own requirements.

**Holdings navigation:** Textron Lycoming Reciprocating Engine Division v. United Automobile Workers — Labor-contract violation jurisdiction.

### Preexisting other coverage and COBRA continuation

**Governing question:** Whether coverage existing before election permits denial or termination of COBRA continuation.

**Current rule:** The applicable 29 U.S.C. §1162(2)(D)(i) permits termination on this branch only when, after election, the beneficiary first becomes covered as an employee or otherwise under another group plan containing no exclusion or limitation concerning any preexisting condition of that beneficiary. Coverage already in force before election, continued coverage or a change in its primacy is not that event.

**Authority by component:**

- Existing other coverage is not a post-election event: Geissal v. Moore Medical Corp. — controlling Holdings, 1998-06-08.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-06-08.

**Exceptions and limits:** All independent eligibility, payment and continuation requirements remain applicable; the rule awards no duplicative benefits or substantive coverage beyond the governing plan and statute.

**Holdings navigation:** Geissal v. Moore Medical Corp. — COBRA continuation and other group coverage.

### Independent EEOC enforcement under the ADEA

**Governing question:** Whether affected employees can prevent an EEOC age-discrimination enforcement action.

**Current rule:** Under §626(b), the EEOC may enforce the ADEA without an affected individual’s charge, consent or request for recovery. Section 626(f)(4) preserves that public authority despite a private waiver, even a valid one. Before suit the Commission must attempt informal conciliation, conference and persuasion, but need not repeat an unproductive offer indefinitely.

**Authority by component:**

- Johnson & Higgins Holding 1: independent enforcement, waiver and actual conciliation: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Johnson & Higgins, Inc. — controlling Holdings, 1998-09-21.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-09-21.

**Exceptions and limits:** Public enforcement authority does not dispense with statutory coverage, liability elements or the basis for the particular remedy.

**Holdings navigation:** Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Johnson & Higgins, Inc. — ADEA enforcement, working owners and compulsory retirement.

### ADEA employee status of corporate owner-directors

**Governing question:** Whether corporate ownership or board membership excludes an otherwise employed person from ADEA coverage.

**Current rule:** Section 630(f)’s circular definition invokes ordinary common-law agency and requires evaluation of all relevant incidents of the actual relationship. Corporate form, an employee label, directorship, ownership, profit-based pay or an exclusive three-factor formula alone cannot decide status. Genuine proprietors remain outside employee coverage, while actual employment may coexist with ownership and governance.

**Authority by component:**

- Johnson & Higgins Holding 2: complete-relationship common-law inquiry: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Johnson & Higgins, Inc. — controlling Holdings, 1998-09-21.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-09-21.

**Exceptions and limits:** Covered employment does not itself guarantee board tenure, ownership rights or any particular compensation.

**Holdings navigation:** Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Johnson & Higgins, Inc. — ADEA enforcement, working owners and compulsory retirement.

### Express age conditions and the executive-retirement exception

**Governing question:** Whether business succession concerns or executive rank justify an express age-based retirement requirement.

**Current rule:** A reasonable business purpose for selecting an express age condition does not make the decision based on a factor other than age under §623(f)(1). Section 631(c) permits compulsory retirement only for an employee who has attained age 65, following bona fide executive or high-policymaking employment throughout the two immediately preceding years, with an immediate nonforfeitable aggregate annual retirement benefit of at least $44,000 from the employer’s pension, profit-sharing, savings or deferred-compensation plans, or their combination. Executive status alone is insufficient.

**Authority by component:**

- Johnson & Higgins Holdings 4–5: age versus other factors and every executive-exception condition: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Johnson & Higgins, Inc. — controlling Holdings, 1998-09-21.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-09-21.

**Exceptions and limits:** Employee coverage and the exception’s complete predicates must independently be established; a governance label cannot substitute for either.

**Controlling construction:** Benefits in another form or involving employee/rollover contributions must receive the prescribed adjustment to a straight-life annuity without ancillary benefits under a plan without employee or rollover contributions.

**Holdings navigation:** Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Johnson & Higgins, Inc. — ADEA enforcement, working owners and compulsory retirement.

### FCA retaliation before or without a successful qui tam action

**Governing question:** Protection of employee investigation or assistance under the then-operative §3730(h).

**Current rule:** Section 3730(h) protects an employee from covered employment retaliation because of lawful acts in furtherance of an FCA action, including qualifying investigation or assistance before filing. The employee must establish protected activity, employer knowledge and causation; protection does not depend solely on successful qui tam recovery or surviving the public-disclosure bar.

**Authority by component:**

- McKenzie Holding 3: independent retaliation conditions: United States ex rel. McKenzie v. BellSouth Telecommunications, Inc. — controlling Holdings, 1998-09-28.

**Present operation effective:** 1998-09-28.

**Exceptions and limits:** Ordinary employment complaints do not become protected solely by their label; ultimate liability and remedies require the applicable statutory proof. The employer need not hear the exact FCA label when the facts convey that the activity concerns contemplated federal enforcement.

**Holdings navigation:** United States ex rel. McKenzie v. BellSouth Telecommunications, Inc. — False Claims Act public disclosure and original-source jurisdiction; United States ex rel. McKenzie v. BellSouth Telecommunications, Inc. — False Claims Act retaliation and independent protected activity.

## Standards and Tests selection: Bankruptcy

## Bankruptcy

### Ordinary-course eligibility of payments on long-term debt

**Governing question:** Whether debt maturity categorically excludes a payment from the contemporaneous §547(c)(2) preference exception.

**Current rule:** Payments on long-term debt may qualify; maturity supplies no additional categorical exclusion or presumption of ordinariness. The creditor bears §547(g)'s burden to prove all three then-current elements: the debt was incurred in the ordinary course of both parties, payment occurred in their ordinary course, and payment accorded with ordinary business terms. Eligibility alone does not establish any element or exempt all interest or commitment fees.

**Authority by component:**

- Long-term-debt eligibility and all retained statutory elements and burden: Union Bank v. Wolas — Law of the decision, Holding and operative rule, December 11, 1991; Stevens's unanimous opinion.

**Present operation effective:** *Wolas*, December 11, 1991.

**Holdings navigation:** Union Bank v. Wolas, 502 U.S. 151 (1991) — Ordinary-course preference exception.

### Chapter 7 strip-down of allowed real-property liens under §506(d)

**Governing question:** Whether §506(d) reduces an allowed, lien-backed real-property debt to its current judicially determined collateral value in the Chapter 7 setting decided in *Dewsnup*.

**Current rule:** When the claim is allowed under §502 and secured by the real-property lien, §506(d) does not strip that lien down merely because §506(a) values the collateral below the allowed debt. Section 506(a) continues to value secured and unsecured amounts for treatment of the claim; that valuation does not automatically avoid the corresponding lien under §506(d). The rule distinguishes personal discharge from lien survival and does not immunize liens from an independently applicable express avoidance provision.

**Authority by component:**

- Limited Chapter 7 construction and continued valuation function: Dewsnup v. Timm — Allowed real-property liens in the presented Chapter 7 setting, January 15, 1992; Blackmun's opinion joined by White, Stevens, O'Connor, and Kennedy.

**Present operation effective:** *Dewsnup*, January 15, 1992.

**Open question:** Other statutory settings, reorganization restrictions, express statutory exceptions, and estate-administration issues are not resolved by this construction. It does not adopt an abandonment rationale.

**Holdings navigation:** Dewsnup v. Timm, 502 U.S. 410 (1992) — Liens and claim valuation.

### Federal sovereign immunity from affirmative bankruptcy money judgments

**Governing question:** Whether original §106(c), estate-property jurisdiction, or property and trust characterizations authorize an affirmative monetary recovery from the United States under §550.

**Current rule:** Original §106(c) does not unequivocally waive immunity from an affirmative personal money judgment recovering an unauthorized transfer under §550. A plausible reading under which its application-and-binding language governs nonmonetary or claim determinations defeats clear consent to that remedy; legislative history cannot supply missing enacted clarity. Sections 106(a) and (b) retain their own claim-linked and offset operations. General estate-property jurisdiction under §1334(d), an asserted trust interest, and the money's origin in estate assets do not supply the missing consent. An order requiring payment of a sum, rather than adjudicating identified property under the court's control, cannot be preserved by calling it a property proceeding or defensive equitable recoupment.

**Authority by component:**

- Original §106(c) monetary-waiver construction: United States v. Nordic Village — Original §106(c) does not clearly authorize this monetary recovery, February 25, 1992.
- Distinction between jurisdiction and consent; inadequacy of property, trust, and recoupment labels: Nordic Village — Jurisdictional and property labels do not sustain this money judgment, February 25, 1992. Scalia's opinion joined by Stone, White, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, and Thomas controls both.

**Present operation effective:** *Nordic Village*, February 25, 1992.

**Open question:** Genuinely distinct specific-property proceedings require their actual facts and independent authority; their validity is not decided. State immunity and a different express statutory waiver remain outside the decision.

**Holdings navigation:** United States v. Nordic Village, Inc., 503 U.S. 30 (1992) — Federal sovereign immunity.

### Ordinary-check transfer date for preference avoidance

**Governing question:** When an ordinary check transfers the debtor's bank-account interest for the preference period in 11 U.S.C. §547(b).

**Current rule:** The transfer occurs when the drawee honors the ordinary check, because delivery gives the payee no assigned interest in the debtor's account. Section 547(e) does not relate the transfer back to a time before that interest passed. The trustee must still establish the other preference elements, and properly presented statutory defenses retain their separate operation. The construction does not decide transfer timing under §547(c) or for nonordinary payment instruments.

**Authority by component:**
- Honor-date construction and preserved boundaries: Barnhill v. Johnson, March 25, 1992, controlling holding 1, “Honor determines the §547(b) transfer”; Stone for White, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Thomas.

**Present operation effective:** Barnhill, March 25, 1992.

**Holdings navigation:** Barnhill v. Johnson, 503 U.S. 393 (1992) — Preference transfer timing.

### Finality of an unchallenged scheduled exemption

**Governing question:** Whether a trustee may contest a scheduled exemption after the applicable Bankruptcy Rule 4003(b) deadline because the claim lacked a colorable statutory basis.

**Current rule:** Under 11 U.S.C. §522(l) and the applicable Rule 4003(b), property claimed as exempt becomes exempt if no party in interest objects within 30 days after the creditors' meeting concludes or a relevant amendment to the exemption list is filed, whichever is later, and no further time is granted within that period. Rule 9006(b)(3) allows enlargement only on Rule 4003(b)'s conditions. Lack of a colorable substantive exemption supplies no exception permitting a later objection. Uncertainty about a scheduled lawsuit's value permits timely inquiry and objection; it does not require waiting for collection. Properly supported misconduct remedies retain their own conditions and do not supply an adjudicated late-objection exception here.

**Authority by component:**
- Deadline, extension, no-objection consequence and rejection of a colorability exception: Taylor v. Freeland & Kronz, April 21, 1992, “Untimely objection to a claimed exemption,” Thomas for Stone, White, Blackmun, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Souter, eight votes.

**Present operation effective:** Taylor, April 21, 1992.

**Exceptions and limits:** The applicable historical deadline governs; the later supplemental-schedule wording does not revive its expiry. Rule 4003(c)'s objector burden remains for timely, properly presented proceedings. This decision concerns the scheduled proceeds claimed and does not determine the scope of differently limited exemption language.

**Open question:** Section 105(a), unpreserved fraud, unscheduled assets, respondents' alternative valuation/lien/good-faith theories, sanctions and retroactivity remain unresolved.

**Holdings navigation:** Taylor v. Freeland & Kronz, 503 U.S. 638 (1992) — Exemption objections.

### Federal-law transfer restrictions and exclusion of trust interests

**Governing question:** Exclusion of a debtor's beneficial trust interest from the estate under 11 U.S.C. §541(c)(2).

**Current rule:** Applicable nonbankruptcy law includes federal law. A transfer restriction on a debtor's beneficial interest in a trust is preserved when enforceable under that law; an established ERISA-qualified trust with an ERISA-enforceable antialienation restriction is therefore excluded from the estate. Exclusion is distinct from exemption and does not change exemption deadlines or adjudicate statutory avoidance remedies.

**Authority by component:**
- Federal-law construction and qualifying trust exclusion: Patterson v. Shumate, “Holding 1: An enforceable federal pension restriction excludes this beneficial trust interest”, June 15, 1992; Blackmun, joined by White, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Thomas (eight).

**Present operation effective:** Patterson v. Shumate, June 15, 1992.

**Open question:** Other plans, nontrust interests, statutory exceptions, distributed benefits, §522(b)(2)(A) and the payment-versus-corpus scope of §522(d)(10)(E) are not decided.

**Holdings navigation:** Patterson v. Shumate, 504 U.S. 753 (1992) — Estate exclusions for pension trust interests.

### Excusable neglect under Rule 9006(b)(1)

**Governing question:** What instructions govern excusable neglect under Rule 9006(b)(1)?

**Current rule:** For a Chapter 11 claim deadline subject to Rule 9006(b)(1), neglect includes inadvertence, mistake and carelessness as well as events beyond control. Post-expiration relief requires a motion and excusability assessed from all relevant circumstances, including debtor prejudice, delay and administrative effects, reason including reasonable control, and good faith. No consideration invariably decides the issue. Freely chosen counsel's conduct is fully attributed to the client; reliance alone is no exception. Under then-effective (b)(2), enlargement is barred for Rules 1007(d), 1017(b)(3), 2003(a) and (d), 7052, 9023 and 9024. Under (b)(3), enlargement is limited to the terms of Rules 1006(b)(2), 1017(e), 3002(c), 4003(b), 4004(a), 4007(c), 8002 and 9033. Thus Chapter 7 claim limits and Taylor's exemption-objection rule gain no general equitable exception.

**Authority by component:**

- 1. Excusable neglect can include carelessness: Pioneer Investment Services Co. v. Brunswick Associates Limited Partnership — 1. Excusable neglect can include carelessness, 1993-03-24. Stone-Zsela's opinion for the Court, joined by White, Blackmun, Stevens and Kennedy: five.
- 2. Counsel's conduct is attributed to the creditor: Pioneer Investment Services Co. v. Brunswick Associates Limited Partnership — 2. Counsel's conduct is attributed to the creditor, 1993-03-24. Stone-Zsela's Court opinion, joined by White, Blackmun, Stevens and Kennedy: five; the dissent does not dispute attorney attribution, but its disagreement about excusability does not create another rationale majority.

**Present operation effective:** 1993-03-24; Pioneer Investment Services Co. v. Brunswick Associates Limited Partnership, for the components identified above.

**Holdings navigation:** Pioneer Investment Services Co. v. Brunswick Associates Limited Partnership, 507 U.S. 380 (1993).

### Principal-residence mortgage rights in Chapter 13

**Governing question:** What instructions govern principal-residence mortgage rights in Chapter 13?

**Current rule:** When an allowed claim secured only by the debtor's principal-residence real property retains a secured portion, §1322(b)(2) protects the holder's mortgage rights as a whole despite §506(a) valuation and bifurcation. The debtor cannot modify the deficiency portion by altering protected repayment or enforcement rights. Independent restrictions and §1322(b)(5) remain: cure within a reasonable time and maintenance during the case are permitted when the last claim payment falls after the final plan payment, not general rewriting. The stay remains distinct. Wholly unsecured liens and classification of ancillary deed provisions are undecided; Dewsnup's Chapter 7 rule remains separate.

**Authority by component:**

- Valuation does not remove the protected rights of this mortgage holder: Nobelman v. American Savings Bank — Valuation does not remove the protected rights of this mortgage holder, 1993-06-01. Thomas’s Opinion of the Court; Stone-Zsela, White, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas (9 Justices). Direct majority support at this level of generality; no Marks synthesis.

**Present operation effective:** 1993-06-01; Nobelman v. American Savings Bank, for the components identified above.

**Holdings navigation:** Nobelman v. American Savings Bank, 508 U.S. 324 (1993).

### Oversecured interest and present value of deferred cure arrearages

**Governing question:** What instructions govern oversecured interest and present value of deferred cure arrearages?

**Current rule:** Section 506(b) allows interest on an allowed secured claim within collateral value exceeding the claim after §506(c) recovery, even without contractual arrearage interest; reasonable fees, costs and charges separately require agreement support. Where §1325(a)(5)(B) governs a deferred secured-arrearage cure over creditor objection with retained collateral, lien retention and effective-date present value of at least the allowed claim are required. Section 1322(b)(5)'s cure-and-maintenance authority does not exempt arrearages; acceptance and surrender are separate alternatives. The parties in Rake accepted §506(b) through confirmation; the Court selects no rate or universal undersecured-mortgage rule.
